audit.recode_to: Un-hedge: weight-sensitive (not 'weight-hedged'), heavy = (C)VC and (C)VV (diphthong or phonemic nasal vowel; allophonic nasalization not heavy), scale (C)VVC > (C)VC > (C)V; default with all-light syllables = left-to-right iambs, final syllable extrametrical, no degenerate feet -> initial in disyllables, second syllable in 3-5-syllable words (the stress window is at the left edge; default_when_no_heavy: second syllable / initial in disyllables, no longer 'CONTESTED'). Deciding source Barros 2016:176-182; keep Green & Green 1997:14 as corroborating (Barros's default pattern is Green's) and Launey 2003:50 as a French-Guiana pedagogical statement whose 'penult if vowel-final' agrees only up to trisyllables and whose 'weak/marginal accent' caveat should stay in the caution/tone note (Silva & Orlando 2025 transcriptions show some final stress on open-final words). Secondary stress: Barros posits iterative iambs (ka.'si.si.pi.te footed (ka.si)(si.pi)<te>) but marks only one prominence; keep 'none described' or note 'feet posited, no secondary prominence transcribed'.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim in copies we hold at the stated places (Green 1997 printed p.14, scanned + page image; Launey 2003 printed p.50, text layer). (2) But both deciding works are pedagogical: a 36-page SIL literacy primer and an IRD learner's introduction; the record is hedged ('weight-hedged', edge 'unclear', default 'CONTESTED') precisely because the two disagree on the default edge and Launey calls the accent marginal. (3) A better source exists and was not yet obtained: Barros da Silva 2016, a UFRJ phonetics/phonology PhD (supervisor Franchetto) with a metrical stress chapter, absent from Glottolog's Palikur bibliography; found via the reference list of Silva & Orlando 2025 (LIAMES) and downloaded from the UFRJ programme page. sources.locator: ch.2 p.59 (review of Green 1997 and Launey 2003 on stress); sec. 6.2.5-6.2.6 pp.176-179 (default position, syllable-weight oppositions); sec. 6.3-6.3.1 pp.179-182 (stress by word length, metrical representation, weight data 403-408, summary list); sec. 5 p.157-158 (nasal vowels attract stress, nasalized vowels do not); ch.7 p.183 (conclusions; notes acoustic study of stress still needed)

sources.quote: No statement of a stress rule. Transcriptions carry stress marks: closed/heavy syllables stressed as in our coding ([pa.ˈkig], [sa.ˈgub], [ig.ˈkis], [ˈkag.ta], nasal-final [ka.ˈɣã]); vowel-final words split between 2nd/penult ([ku.ˈɣu.ku], [si.ˈva.gi], [pa.ˈɣa.ka], [a.ˈvi.ɣi]) and final ([a.gi.ˈku], [tu.gu.ˈhɛ], [u.gu.ˈkɛ], [a.ɣa.ˈku], [a.mad.ˈga], [gaw.na.sãn.ˈvu], [gi.kẽn.ˈgi], [a.ma.ˈbɔ]) — data only, consistent with Launey's remark that the accent is weak/variable.
